title: Oscar and the Atlas
premise: In the winter of 1792, in the river city of Vellmark, Coral Dravenmoor works her late father's type cases in a print shop that quietly serves both sides of an approaching revolution. When an infant boy is abandoned at the shop's door wrapped in seditious pamphlets — evidence that could topple Governor Atlas Corvane — Coral becomes the unwilling courier who must carry proof of Corvane's massacres past three military checkpoints before New Year's Eve. Betrayed by the printer she trusted and hunted by the governor's spymaster, she discovers the child is Corvane's own grandson, smuggled out by his daughter to end the dynasty's bloodline of cruelty. In the end Coral delivers neither the child nor the pamphlets to any faction: she prints the truth herself on the old press, burns the original evidence, and gives the boy to a family across the border, choosing belonging over survival — at the cost of her shop, her city, and the only life she knew.
about_author: Sebastian Eriksen is the pen name of a former letterpress compositor who spent a decade restoring nineteenth-century printing equipment in Baltic port towns. His novels are known for their tactile detail and their fascination with ordinary people caught between history's grinding wheels.

chapters.title: The Smell of Ink and Iron
chapters.summary: Coral Dravenmoor's POV. Establishes the print shop, her dead father's type cases, and the city's uneasy quiet under Governor Corvane. She keeps her head down, setting type for whoever pays. Emotional beat: weary self-containment, the comfort of routine on the edge of chaos.

chapters.title: A Bundle at the Door
chapters.summary: On a freezing December night, Coral finds an infant wrapped in a blanket lined with pamphlets describing a massacre at Hallow Bridge. A note reads: forget the face. Her employer, Master Quillon, orders her to burn everything. Emotional beat: dread cracking open her careful neutrality.

chapters.title: What the Pamphlets Say
chapters.summary: Coral secretly reads the pamphlets by candlelight — names, dates, orders signed by Corvane himself. Quillon's nervousness suggests he knows more than he admits. POV shifts briefly to Quillon. Emotional beat: the seduction and terror of knowing too much.

chapters.title: The First Checkpoint
chapters.summary: Sent on a routine delivery, Coral realizes she is being tested: soldiers search her cart while the pamphlets sit beneath the floorboards with the sleeping child hidden in the type chest. She passes by luck and a soldier's boredom. Emotional beat: white-knuckle fear, first taste of deception.

chapters.title: Master Quillon's Bargain
chapters.summary: Quillon reveals he has been printing for the resistance for years and now wants Coral to carry the full evidence packet to a contact beyond the river before the year turns. He offers her the shop as payment. Emotional beat: reluctant ambition — she wants to belong to something.

chapters.title: The Spymaster's Visit
chapters.summary: Corvane's spymaster, Herron Vail, inspects the shop, lingering over Coral's father's tools. He mentions a missing child and missing papers, watching her face. POV alternates with Vail's cold interiority. Emotional beat: being seen through, the hunter's patience.

chapters.title: Milk, Type, and Lies
chapters.summary: A quieter chapter: Coral cares for the baby among the galley trays, naming him privately 'Atlas' as a bitter joke. A neighbor, the midwife Sera Ondel, begins to suspect and then to help. Emotional beat: unexpected tenderness, the beginnings of belonging.

chapters.title: The Resistance Contact
chapters.summary: Coral meets the resistance liaison, a bookseller named Ivor Kade, who turns out to know her father's past — and hints her father died for printing truths like these. Emotional beat: grief reframed; her inheritance is larger than type metal.

chapters.title: Betrayal in the Composing Room
chapters.summary: Quillon sells the route to Vail to save his own skin. Coral learns of it from a drunk apprentice and must move the child and evidence that night. Emotional beat: fury and abandonment; trust becomes a currency she can no longer afford.

chapters.title: Through the Tanner's Quarter
chapters.summary: Flight sequence: Coral and the baby cross the tannery district through smoke and frozen mud, aided by Sera. Vail's men sweep behind them. Emotional beat: survival stripped to instinct; the price of every kindness made visible.

chapters.title: The Second Checkpoint
chapters.summary: At the river gate, Coral hides the pamphlets inside a coffin being shipped for burial, riding with the grieving family. The guard is Corvane's own nephew, and he hesitates — a crack in the regime shown from within. Emotional beat: grim irony; even power's servants doubt.

chapters.title: Whose Child Is This?
chapters.summary: Ivor reveals the truth: the baby is Corvane's grandson, carried out by the governor's daughter Lysandra to break the line of tyrants. Coral must decide if the child is cargo, weapon, or simply a child. Emotional beat: moral vertigo; the evidence has a heartbeat.

chapters.title: Lysandra's Letter
chapters.summary: Hidden in the blanket lining, Coral finds Lysandra's confession — her father killed Coral's father's generation of printers, and she cannot raise a son on that throne. POV interlude in Lysandra's voice. Emotional beat: sorrow bridging enemy lines; two fathers, two daughters.

chapters.title: Vail Closes the Net
chapters.summary: Vail arrests Quillon and tortures him for Coral's route. Quillon, broken, gives up half the truth. Coral, warned by the apprentice, goes to ground in the print shop's cellar. Emotional beat: claustrophobia; the cost of other people's fear.

chapters.title: The Third Checkpoint
chapters.summary: The mountain pass tollhouse, last barrier before the border. Coral poses as a widow traveling to her sister's; the checkpoint commander demands she surrender the 'stolen' infant — Vail's description has reached him. Emotional beat: the longest night; wit against armed authority.

chapters.title: What Survival Costs
chapters.summary: Coral pays the commander with her father's silver type punch — the last thing she owns of him — to look away. Crossing the pass, she weeps for the first time since the door. Emotional beat: the theme made flesh; survival always takes a piece of you.

chapters.title: The Empty Cradle
chapters.summary: At the safe house, resistance hardliners reveal they intend to use the child as a figurehead — another kind of cage. Coral refuses to hand him over. Ivor is torn between cause and conscience. Emotional beat: disillusionment; revolution can corrupt like any crown.

chapters.title: Back Across the River
chapters.summary: Coral slips back into occupied Vellmark alone, leaving the baby with Sera, to retrieve the one thing the resistance doesn't have: the original press proofs bearing Corvane's signature. Emotional beat: reversal — the fugitive returns as the hunter.

chapters.title: The Press in the Cellar
chapters.summary: Coral breaks into her own shop, now Vail's headquarters, and finds Quillon dying among the type cases. He begs forgiveness; she sets his last words in type instead. She pulls the proofs as Vail descends the stairs. Emotional beat: climax begins; mercy as defiance.

chapters.title: New Year's Eve
chapters.summary: Cornered in the cellar, Coral triggers the press's counterweight, trapping Vail beneath the frame, and escapes through the coal chute as midnight bells ring. The century turns without her delivering anything to anyone. Emotional beat: catharsis; the machine of power literally brought down by its own weight.

chapters.title: Ten Thousand Copies
chapters.summary: From a barn across the border, Coral prints the massacre evidence herself — ten thousand copies scattered through Vellmark by Ivor's network. Corvane falls not to armies but to ink. She burns the originals so no faction can ever own the truth again. Emotional beat: triumph without victory-lust; truth belongs to everyone or no one.

chapters.title: Oscar and the Atlas
chapters.summary: Spring. Coral, nameless in a border village, visits the farm family raising the boy — whom she finally names Oscar, after her father. She does not tell them who he was. Holding him once, she lets go. Final image: her hands setting type again, empty of everything but the work. Emotional beat: belonging chosen freely; the price paid, and worth it.
